title: Joash Repairs the Temple
summary: Joash reigns forty years in Jerusalem and does what is right while the priest Jehoiada instructs him, though the high places remain. He orders the priests to use temple income for repairs, and when nothing has been done by his twenty-third year, a collection chest is set beside the altar and the money is paid directly to the workmen. Later, when Hazael of Aram takes Gath and threatens Jerusalem, Joash buys him off with the temple and palace treasures, and in the end Joash is assassinated by his own servants.
story: The boy rescued and crowned in chapter 11 now grows up and reigns. The covenant renewal Jehoiada led, and the destruction of Baal's temple in Jerusalem, leads naturally to the restoration of the LORD's temple, which had been neglected and, according to 2 Chronicles 24:7, plundered by Athaliah's sons for the service of Baal. The chapter shows a reform that is real but limited. The temple is repaired and the money is handled honestly, yet the high places stay, the treasures are later given away to a foreign king, and Joash dies by conspiracy. Joash's son Amaziah succeeds him, and the next chapters return to Israel under Jehu's descendants.
historical:
Joash (also spelled Jehoash) reigned in Judah about 835 to 796 BC. His reign overlapped with Jehu and his son Jehoahaz in Israel, a period when Hazael of Damascus dominated the region. Hazael's capture of Gath (verse 17), one of the chief Philistine cities, fits what archaeologists have found at Tell es-Safi, generally identified as Gath: a siege trench around the city and a destruction layer from the late ninth century BC, which the excavators attribute to Hazael's campaign. Jerusalem lay only about twenty-five miles to the east, and Joash chose to pay rather than fight.

Solomon's temple was by now well over a century old, and repairs to stone, timber, and fittings were needed. Second Chronicles 24 tells more of Joash's story. After Jehoiada died, Joash and the officials of Judah turned to idols, and when Jehoiada's son Zechariah rebuked them, Joash had him stoned in the temple court. The Chronicler presents the Aramean attack and Joash's assassination as judgments for that act. Second Kings does not mention these events, but its phrasing in verse 2, that Joash did right all the days Jehoiada instructed him, hints that his later years were different. The locations Beth-millo and Silla are not known with certainty.
cultural:
The temple received several kinds of income. The census money was the half-shekel ransom paid for each person counted (Exodus 30:12-16); vow money came from valuations set on people or things dedicated to the LORD (Leviticus 27); and freewill gifts were voluntary. Coins were not yet in use in Judah, so money meant weighed pieces of silver, which is why the royal scribe and the high priest counted it and tied it in bags (verse 10). The priests' constituency, or acquaintances, were probably the worshipers each priest dealt with, from whom he received offerings.

The chest with a hole bored in its lid, set by the altar, removed the money from the priests' handling and made the giving public and accountable. The workers named (carpenters, builders, masons, stonecutters) were skilled craftsmen who had to be paid in silver. Verse 15 notes that no accounting was demanded of the supervisors because they dealt faithfully, a striking note of trust. The guilt and sin offering money (verse 16) stayed with the priests, as the law provided for their support (compare Leviticus 5:16 and 7:7).
literary: The chapter opens and closes with the regnal formula for Joash, framing a reign described mainly by one project. The account of the temple repair is unusually detailed and practical, full of administrative language: collection, accounting, supervision, payment. Its key word is the breach or damage (bedeq) of the temple, repeated through verses 5-12. The account also contains a quiet criticism: the priests had taken the money for twenty-three years and done nothing. The narrator contrasts two uses of sacred treasures. In the first half, the gifts of the people repair the LORD's house; in verse 18, the dedicated gifts of Joash and his fathers are sent away to buy off Hazael. The ending is abrupt, with conspirators named and no reason given, a pattern that becomes common in the later chapters of Kings.

outline.t: The priests fail to repair the temple
The collection chest and the honest repair of the temple
Hazael threatens Jerusalem and is paid off
Joash is assassinated and Amaziah succeeds him

doctrines.note: The care of the house of worship is the shared work of king, priests, people, and craftsmen. The chapter treats practical stewardship of money and buildings, done with integrity, as part of faithfulness to God.
The repair of the temple follows the covenant renewal of chapter 11. Restoring the place where God is worshiped expresses the people's renewed commitment to be the LORD's people.

Joash did right while Jehoiada instructed him (verse 2). The phrase raises the question of borrowed faith: a life shaped by a mentor's convictions that may not hold when the mentor is gone, as 2 Chronicles 24 shows.

words.note: Bedeq, a breach, crack, or damaged place in a building, used seven times in this chapter and almost nowhere else. The repetition shows the narrator's concern: the LORD's house had been allowed to fall into disrepair, and the repairs were a sign of renewed care for his worship.

Aron, chest or box. It is the same word used for the ark of the covenant, though here it names a simple collection chest by the altar. The ordinary use reminds a reader that the ark itself was a box; its holiness came from what it held and what God did there.

Emunah, faithfulness or integrity, related to the word amen. The supervisors were not required to give an accounting because they acted with emunah (verse 15). The word is used of God's own faithfulness and of the faith by which the righteous live (Habakkuk 2:4).

christ: The temple, whose repair fills this chapter, is a central image for the New Testament's understanding of Jesus, who spoke of his body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19-21). The collection chests of the later temple appear in the Gospels when Jesus watches people giving at the treasury and praises the widow who gave two small coins, all she had (Mark 12:41-44). Jesus also refers to the murder of Zechariah between the altar and the sanctuary (Luke 11:51; compare Matthew 23:35), which many interpreters identify with the son of Jehoiada killed on Joash's orders according to 2 Chronicles 24:20-22, as the last martyr named in the Hebrew Bible's order of books. These links are thematic and historical rather than predictive, and they connect the story of the temple's care and its guardians' failures to Jesus' own judgment on the temple of his day.

hard.q: Why does 2 Kings describe Joash so favorably when 2 Chronicles says he turned to idols and killed the prophet Zechariah?
hard.a: Second Kings says Joash did right all the days Jehoiada instructed him and focuses on his temple repair, the payment to Hazael, and his assassination. Second Chronicles 24 adds that after Jehoiada's death Joash listened to officials who turned to idols, had Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned in the temple court when he rebuked them, and was killed by servants avenging Zechariah's blood. The two accounts are usually seen as complementary rather than contradictory. The writer of Kings selects events to fit his concern with worship and the temple, and his careful wording in verse 2 leaves room for a later decline. The Chronicler, writing later for the community after the exile, draws out the moral pattern of Joash's life more fully: faithfulness under a mentor, apostasy afterward, and judgment. Some scholars think the Chronicler had access to additional sources; others think he interpreted the events theologically. Both works agree on the main shape: a good beginning, a temple restored, Aramean pressure, and a violent end.

questions: The priests collected money for twenty-three years without repairing the temple. What structures of accountability help good intentions actually get carried out?
Joash did right while Jehoiada instructed him. How can a person move from borrowed faith to convictions of their own?
Joash used the dedicated treasures to buy off Hazael. When is it wise to give up what is precious to avoid a greater harm, and when does it become a failure of trust in God?
